entries.title: Trump Claws Back Nearly $1 Billion in Congressionally Appropriated Funding
entries.summary: The administration is using a rare and contested power to ax funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives.
entries.content:
By Kevin Freking

President Donald Trump is canceling nearly $1 billion in spending approved by Congress, the White House announced on Friday, using a rare and contested power to ax funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives.

Trump's Office of Management and Budget described the funding cut as focused on “the most harmful government spending.”

Most of the cuts are focused on services for immigrants, including nonprofits that serve refugees and unaccompanied minors accused of being in the country illegally. The administration says the funds are no longer necessary because illegal border crossings have diminished considerably.

A White House press release announcing the funding rescissions notes that some of the organizations are led by people who worked in the administration of Democratic President Barack Obama.

Trump’s move was condemned by Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican in a tough re-election campaign and chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.

Collins said in a statement that the action came without warning or consultation. She also said she would work to address with colleagues “these illegal actions.”

“Not only is the delay itself an impoundment that was not reported to Congress, but also it is a usurpation of Congress’s appropriations powers,” Collins said. “OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding."

Typically, Congress can review the president’s proposed spending cuts before they take effect. But Trump made that all but impossible by announcing them with just five days left in the federal fiscal year. The Government Accountability Office says the maneuver, known as a “pocket rescission,” is illegal.

Collins called it the latest attempt by OMB to “undermine Congress’s Constitutional power of the purse.”

A year ago, Trump issued a pocket rescission for the first time in 50 years by blocking $4.9 billion in congressionally approved foreign aid. The U.S. Supreme Court declined to block those rescissions, saying that Trump’s authority over foreign affairs weighed heavily in its decision. This year, Trump is targeting domestic spending.

The use of a pocket rescission fits part a broader pattern by the Trump administration to exact greater control over the U.S. government, eroding the power of Congress.

The administration has also fired federal workers, imposed a historic increase in tariffs, and started the war in Iran without going through Congress, putting the burden on the judicial branch to determine the limits of presidential power.

entries.title: Elena Delle Donne Isn’t Coming Back. Not That She Hasn’t Thought About It.
entries.summary: The Mystics legend, whose jump shot is still as good as ever, is the link between the 2019 championship squad and 2026 playoff team.
entries.content:
The adrenaline was still there. The joy was still there. And lo and behold, the shot was still there, arcing over and over from Elena Delle Donne’s fingertips to the bottom of the net. With the familiar butterflies running through her and her senses reengaged — the tacky grip of the basketball, the cacophony of the crowd, the sharp-edged geometry of the court — it was only natural that a voice in her head would cut through the chaos of WNBA’s All-Star Weekend and whisper: “You could still have this.”

It was July 24, and Delle Donne, who last played for the Washington Mystics in 2023 and officially retired in 2024, had just teamed with former Mystics teammate Shakira Austin and high school phenom Jezelle “GG” Banks at Chicago’s Wintrust Arena to win the WNBA Shooting Stars competition — a contest bringing together a retired legend, a current player and a prospect from each city in the league. All anybody wanted to know, including the voice in Delle Donne’s own head, was whether she might consider a comeback.

“There will always be a spot for her on the court in Washington if she wants it!” Mystics owner Ted Leonsis posted on X.

It was — and remains — a tantalizing thought. As the 2026 Mystics, those youthful, exuberant upstarts, prepare to open the WNBA playoffs against Atlanta, the centerpiece of their last great team, the 2019 league champions, has reemerged into the public spotlight after several years spent largely out of view. She had no choice: This summer alone, aside from the nationally televised Shooting Stars victory, Delle Donne was inducted into no fewer than three halls of fame.

All other things being equal, Delle Donne would rather be getting ready for another deep playoff run than writing hall of fame speeches and being asked about her legacy. A few weeks past her 37th birthday, Delle Donne wouldn’t even be the oldest player in the WNBA this season — that would be 39-year-old Alysha Clark of the Dallas Wings — a reality that only dials up the pull the game still exerts on her.

“For the rest of my life, I’m going to consider playing,” she told The Washington Sun. “It’s such a part of you. To have the crowd behind you, to go out and win a championship — those things are so exciting and fun. Of course, you think about it: Do I still have it? Could I push through everything? So yeah, you question it. It’s only human.

“But the reality is, when the next day you wake up and it’s, ‘Ugh, my back,’ and I’ve got a kink in my neck from sleeping on it wrong – that’s when you get brought back to reality. I certainly wish I could still be playing. I feel like skills-wise, I still have it. It’s just that my body doesn’t have it.”

And so, when the Mystics take the floor for their playoff opener, Delle Donne, a special adviser to Monumental Basketball (the Mystics’ parent company), will remain behind the scenes. While her role, by design, is largely undefined, encompassing elements of scouting, coaching and executive strategizing, she thinks of herself mostly as a liaison between the coaching staff and the Mystics’ players, who collectively make up the youngest roster in the league. Two of those players are her former teammates: Austin, whose first two seasons with the Mystics, 2022 and 2023, were Delle Donne’s last two, and guard Betnijah Laney-Hamilton, with whom she played two seasons in Chicago.

“You get to see what the front office goes through. You get to work with the coaching staff,” Delle Donne said of her Monumental gig. “But my favorite part is going to practice and interacting with the players and staff — seeing that growth over the course of a season and trying to give each player a piece of something to help them in life or on the court, whatever that might be.”

There are few obvious parallels between the veteran-laden Mystics team that won the title in 2019 and the youthful upstarts of 2026, but Delle Donne has taken note of an important one:

“The love for each other,” she said. “That’s how we were [in 2019], and more than anything else, that’s what I see in this team: the selflessness and the caring about the person next to you. It means way more than any individual accolade anyone gets.”

‘There’s Other Life to Be Had’

The 2019 Mystics season was the high-water mark of Delle Donne’s dazzling career, culminating in not only her second MVP award but her one and only championship. She became the first WNBA player in history to shoot better than 50% on field goals, 40% on three-pointers and 90% on free throws. (Her career free-throw success rate of 93.7% remains the best in history by anyone in either the WNBA or NBA.)

But she also spent much of that season in excruciating pain from a back injury that required three surgeries to repair herniated discs after the season ended, while also dealing with lingering effects from Lyme disease, which has afflicted her since childhood, requiring a daily regimen of 50 pills and supplements to counteract it.

“Thank God we won a championship,” she said of those 2019 Mystics, “because I put my back on the line for that one.”

She would play three more seasons — opting out of the 2020 “bubble” season during the pandemic — then went more or less off the grid, disappearing into family life (she married her partner, Amanda Clifton, in 2017) and eventually finding behind-the-scenes roles within the game, both with Monumental and with USA Basketball as the managing director of the women’s 3x3 National Team.

“I didn’t want to be a player who hung around until the wheels literally fell off,” she said. “I know there’s other life to be had. Who knows? Hopefully there are kids down the road. I want to be able to play with them and not be in constant pain. I had done all I could [as a player] in the sport.”

She might have stayed out of the public eye forever if it weren’t for the various halls of fame lining up to bestow a measure of immortality upon her this summer. It started on June 27 with the Women’s Basketball Hall of Fame in Knoxville, Tennessee, where she was inducted as part of a class that also included fellow WNBA legend Candace Parker, broadcaster Doris Burke and longtime Minnesota Lynx head coach Cheryl Reeve.

Next up, on Aug. 15, was the big one: the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame in Springfield, Massachusetts, where her induction class included Parker, fellow Mystics standout Chamique Holdsclaw and longtime NBA player and championship-winning coach Doc Rivers.

By the time the D.C. Sports Hall of Fame called and told Delle Donne she would be inducted on Aug. 30 — along with NFL linebacker London Fletcher and basketball standout turned coach Tommy Amaker, among others — it was starting to feel a little ridiculous.

“I’d call my family and be like, ‘Hey, we have another hall of fame,’” she said. “They’re like, ‘Wait, what’s this one?’ And I’m like, ‘I didn’t realize there were this many either. But hey, we’re doing it.’... I’ve never been one to talk much about myself. But you kind of have to when you’re going into the Hall of Fame. I definitely tried to make my speeches about the bigger lessons I learned by playing sports.”

‘They’re Getting What They Deserve’

Those honors, however overwhelming when taken together, seemed like well-deserved milestones in the post-playing life of a sports legend.

But in the middle of all that legacy-burnishing, Delle Donne got the call asking her to participate in the Shooting Stars competition during All-Star Weekend. At the time, she had barely picked up a basketball in three years, her on-court activity limited to occasionally guarding and rebounding for her 13-year-old niece Gia during the teen’s workouts. Had that remained the full extent of her on-court participation in basketball, she would have been perfectly content.

Being back on the court in Chicago, however, and back in the public spotlight, was a revelation in several ways for Delle Donne, with none more powerful than the mixture of awe and pride she felt at how huge the WNBA’s All-Star extravaganza had become: a full weekend of events featuring first-class treatment for participants and massive crowds everywhere — capped by the All-Star Game itself, with nearly 20,000 spectators jammed into the arena.

It was a far cry from the way she remembers All-Star Games from early in her career, which, she said, felt like “a scrimmage that was just thrown together, and hopefully people will show up.”

In 2013, Delle Donne’s rookie year with the Chicago Sky, the league averaged about 7,500 fans per game, with none of the league’s 12 teams averaging more than 10,000. But this year, with the WNBA having expanded to 15 teams (and with three more on the way), average attendance is 11,482, with 10 teams averaging more than 10,000, led by the Golden State Valkyries at 18,064 per game.

“The level of play has always been there, and it was just so hard to understand the lag of getting the media attention, getting businesses to buy in, getting eyes on our game,” Delle Donne said. “I knew it was the greatest product, and when people watched it, they loved it. But when I was playing, most of the time you couldn’t find it on TV … It was so frustrating that it didn’t have that ‘cool’ factor.

“We got the message all the time from [league] leadership: ‘You need to do all these things or we’re folding. You have to save the game.’ And it was always so frustrating to be like: ‘Why can’t our greatness on the court be enough?’ And I’m so glad it is enough now.”

Everything — the All-Star experience, the Mystics’ summer surge to the playoffs, the realization that her shot was as beautiful and effective as ever — conspired to raise the volume of that voice in her head, the one telling her she could still mount a comeback.

In the end, though, it was not only the back pain that kept Delle Donne from heeding that call. It was also the constant reflection on her legacy, necessitated by all those hall of fame speeches, plus her firsthand look in Chicago at what that legacy had helped achieve: a league that is exploding with growth; record attendance and television ratings; a new collective-bargaining agreement that has seen player salaries increase exponentially.

“I’m so proud of the people who came before me, the people of my era who played and are still playing, and the younger generation,” she said. “They’re getting what they deserve.”

Maybe Delle Donne also deserved a taste of it. But that’s what she got in Chicago. And she did it without sacrificing her health. Her balky back is quiet for the moment. Maybe someday soon, the voice in her head will be, too.
entries.author: Dave Sheinin

entries.title: Marcus Mariota Has Prepared to Be a Starter. Now’s His Chance.
entries.summary: The 12-year veteran will fill in for injured starter Jayden Daniels on Sunday against the Seahawks.
entries.content:
If Marcus Mariota has learned anything over the past couple of seasons, it was a lesson taught by Southern California rapper Suga Free almost 30 years ago.

“If you stay ready,” Suga Free said on the 1997 track of the same name, “You ain’t got to get ready.”

The Commanders backup quarterback will be filling in for starter Jayden Daniels this Sunday against the defending champion Seahawks after Daniels dislocated his left elbow last week. This will be a bit of déjà vu for Mariota, as he started eight games — and appeared in another three — last season due to various injuries to Daniels.

The 12-year veteran said he’s learned over the seasons that always being prepared to play makes the suddenness of being thrust into the starting lineup more manageable.

“Being in this position for the last seven years or so in my career, you never know when your number's gonna be called,” Mariota said this week. “So, I just try to treat every week like I'm the starter and I just kind of mentally prepare that way so that if it does happen, the transition's relatively easy.”

That’s of course easier said than done with the Commanders at 0-2 and welcoming a 2-0 Seattle team that beat them 38-14 last season. But in a league that lives by the creed “next man up,” Mariota is expected to come and produce however he can.

After the Cowboys game, head coach Dan Quinn said the team would rally around Mariota, and that they want to make the transition from Daniels to him as seamless as possible. Nearly everyone on the roster has emphasized how much faith and trust they have in Mariota.

The key to keeping this season from getting too far off track with Sunday’s game and a trip to London next week to play the Colts is for Mariota to play within himself and trust his teammates. This is a new thought process for Mariota. In the past he’d feel he needed to come in, put the offense on his back and play the hero. That would at times lead to disastrous results.

“Stepping in some of those games, you feel like you have to kind of make a play and sometimes you overstress yourself — and now you're making a mistake, you're fumbling the football, you're throwing a pick,” Mariota said.

“I took a lot of those lessons and with what happened on the game on Sunday, and was able to kind of stay within myself, play the game that I know how to play, and it really kind of led to some success,” he continued. “So, the more that I can kind of focus on those types of things, not put the cape on as people say, and just allow everybody else in the offense to work for us, I think the better that I'll play and the better the position for our offense.”

This week, Mariota has held conversations with the receivers about route mechanics and ways to exploit the Seattle defense, and he went over pass protection with the running backs. Mariota was late to his first presser as the starter on Wednesday while putting in extra work after practice.

“We have full confidence in what he can do,” wide receiver Terry McLaurin said. “The way he runs the offense is very succinct. The way he communicates in the huddle is very clear. And he brings a calm to the huddle that is expected from a guy like Marcus.”

When receiver Stefon Diggs first signed with the team in early August, he spent a lot of time running plays with Mariota and the second unit as he got acclimated.

“He's a good quarterback. He's been in this league for a long time. Got a lot of confidence in him,” said Diggs, who caught Mariota’s lone touchdown in Dallas. “As a receiver, you just got to go in with the right mindset of getting open, catching the ball. It's still football at the end of the day and you want to be open for him.”

Quinn said on Monday there will be no “pullback” on the playbook with Mariota, while offensive coordinator David Blough said he can't wait to “turn him loose.” Mariota will give his input on what works for him and what doesn’t, but he doesn’t expect things to be fully catered to his needs.

“Part of the backup role is you kinda fill that need, right? You're gonna like a lot of the stuff that Jay likes,” Mariota said. “There is a little bit of differences here and there, but the role as the backup is when you get called upon, it's not a huge difference.”

In 11 appearances last season, including the eight games he started, Mariota completed 61.2% of his passes for 1,695 yards, 10 touchdowns and seven interceptions. But he was considerably better in plays where he took a three-step dropback, identified his first read and got the ball out.

On passes thrown 2.5 seconds or less following the snap, Mariota completed 71% of 107 passes for 607 yards, five touchdowns and two interceptions, according to NFL Research. His 92.7 passer rating on quick throws was similar to starters Justin Herbert (93.5) and Trevor Lawrence (93.5).

“I really think of myself as a point guard. The more that I can get these guys the ball, the playmakers, especially faster, the more space they get, the more that they can do with it,” Mariota said. “I used to joke like they tackle the guy with the ball, so the more that I can get it out of my hand, by all means.”

Against a Seattle defense that allows the fewest yards per play (3.8) in the NFL, the Commanders will need to lean on Mariota’s strengths. But Washington can take deep shots when given the opening. Blough said Mariota’s experience means he knows when the ball should leave his hands and at what trajectory the ball should take. He averaged the furthest intended air yards (10.2) of any quarterback last season, according to NFL Research.

Facing a single-high safety against the Raiders in Week 3 last season, he came out of his dropback and hit McLaurin for a 56-yard touchdown. Seven weeks later the Lions sent a six-man blitz at Mariota, who set his feet, took a bump from a defender and hit Treylon Burks in stride for a 37-yard grab.

On slower-developing plays, Mariota is adept at moving around the pocket to buy time. He exhibited that on multiple occasions against the Cowboys last week, evading the Dallas pass rush.

“The second play has always been sometimes your biggest plays, your most explosive plays, and the quarterback position has transitioned into those types of players,” Mariota said. “I've always kind of felt like I've been that way.”

Broken plays can also lead to mistakes, like during Week 13 against Denver last season when he got pressured in the pocket and had nowhere to throw the ball. Rather than toss it out of bounds and give the offense a chance on third down, he instead threw it into double coverage and was intercepted.

But he believes he’s learned from those mistakes as he once again takes the reins in Washington.

“I thought last week, being able to come in and not overstress and just be like, ‘Hey, just go and play within the system,’” Mariota said. “That was a big step for me because I think as a backup you're like, ‘I gotta go make a play. I gotta try to help these teams win.’”
entries.author: Martenzie Johnson

entries.title: Trump Courted Xi. MAGAworld Stewed.
entries.summary: White House aides say the president has been tougher on China than any recent administration.
entries.content:
Top allies of President Donald Trump were alarmed by his conciliatory approach toward Chinese President Xi Jinping this week, with the concern privately running deeper than public comments suggested, according to more than a dozen interviews with administration officials, lawmakers and policy experts.

Trump gave Xi an extraordinary welcome, including a formal state dinner with business titans, a military flyover and a tour of the National Archives. Xi’s first visit in more than a decade came as the White House had dropped its most aggressive economic penalties on China and aimed to reduce tensions between the world’s two great superpowers.

The perceived turnabout in both policy and rhetoric toward China — which Trump once accused of "raping" the U.S. economically — unsettled many of Trump’s supporters who previously thrilled to his adversarial posture toward Beijing.

Steve Bannon, the president’s former chief strategist and a top China critic, publicly called for no concessions to the Chinese on his podcast for three consecutive days during Xi’s visit, and privately relayed that message to administration officials. Senate Republicans who rarely publicly break with the president bashed the “lavish welcome.” And Laura Loomer, typically one of the president’s most ardent defenders on social media, slammed the “red carpet treatment” and “win for our enemies.”

Meanwhile, one White House official told The Washington Sun that there was broad concern among the administration’s China hawks.

“It is astonishing what is going on right now — Trump is functionally a China dove right now,” said one administration ally granted anonymity to speak candidly.

The White House strongly rejected these characterizations.

White House aide Peter Navarro, widely regarded as the fiercest China hawk in the president’s orbit, said he was consulted on the summit and supported it. The goal was to eliminate the “obvious disconnect” between the commitments Xi has made to the president and China’s refusal to fulfill those obligations thus far, Navarro said.

Navarro also stressed that the president has imposed 50% tariffs on many imports from China, and pointed out that industry-specific duties allow that number to be even higher.

“Frequent one-on-one meetings allow POTUS to express obvious concern and at times displeasure with promises made but unkept, and this helps keep things on track,” Navarro said in a statement. “I’m a veteran of the first Trump White House and the China wars. The best path is action, action, action — talk softly but move fast.”

On Friday, the president said American farmers would be “very happy” with the result of the talks — appearing to preview new Chinese purchases of U.S. agricultural products — while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pushed for a new hotline between the countries’ leadership for emergencies related to artificial intelligence.

Of the criticism that Xi was treated with too much deference and praise, Navarro said: “You don’t do a major state visit of a world leader without red carpet treatment.”

Still, this week’s tone and strategy affirm the extent to which Trump, faced with the political realities of a trade war, has reversed his posture on one of the most important economic policies of his tenure.

Michael Pillsbury, who served as chair of the Pentagon’s Defense Policy Board, said Trump has privately recognized the upside of a more pragmatic response to Beijing.

“I have had a chance to speak directly to him. He thinks the first-term was too confrontational to get results,” Pillsbury said. Of the traditional China hawks in Trump’s orbit, Pillsbury said: “This group is no longer very powerful. … Are they upset? Yes, but they’re very careful to not dare attack Trump directly.”
Trump (4928x3290, AR: 1.50)In his first-term, Trump imposed new tariffs and economic sanctions on China. Those policies were largely maintained by the Biden administration. The initial moves of Trump’s second term suggested he only wanted to amplify that approach, imposing sky-high tariffs on China, and the rest of the world, in April 2025.

But after China retaliated by restricting American access to rare earth minerals crucial for a range of domestic products, the U.S. economy faced a full-blown economic crisis. The moment crystallized the economic and political limitations Trump faces in trying to untangle the world’s two largest economies, and has been only followed by a gradual easing of tariffs and sanctions between the countries.

Edward Fishman, senior fellow and director of the Maurice R. Greenberg Center for Geoeconomics at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the Chinese response to Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs caused a reaction that set the stage for this week’s summit.

“It was a crisis of confidence in the White House, and where we’ve been ever since is this effective detente,” Fishman said. “There’s been a sea change in U.S. policy toward China, and there’s real concern that taking aggressive action against them will result in retaliation that the United States can’t sustain.”

Navarro said the administration is working with a “large team” and more than 50 companies to reduce U.S. dependence on Chinese rare earth metals, which will give it the capacity to confront China without fear of blowback. On Friday, Navarro said on Bannon’s podcast that the U.S. is between six and 18 months of being “rare earth magnet independent. (Bannon described Navarro’s prediction as “impossible.”)

Some former Trump administration officials have said Navarro’s influence appears to be on the decline as the president works with Xi.

“Peter has certainly not been very outspoken of late — whether that’s because he’s been sidelined, or what it is I don’t know,” said Wilbur Ross, who served as Commerce secretary during Trump’s first term and was widely seen as largely sympathetic to Navarro’s goals. “Normally, in the context of the China meeting you would have thought there would be some commentary from him.”

Navarro said his public communications have “of course” not been limited, citing appearances on MS NOW, Bloomberg and CNBC, among other outlets.

The concerns about Trump’s invitation to Xi may run deepest on Capitol Hill. Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker of Mississippi criticized the president in a floor speech in which he said he would have recommended against the Xi visit and that he would remind the president “his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America.”

Lawmakers in both parties are concerned about Trump’s decision to delay $14 billion in arms sales for Taiwan. Adam Posen, an economist at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, said it’s possible Congress will force the president to adopt tougher economic and foreign policy measures against Beijing next year, after the midterm elections.

But for now, Posen, who favors reduced trade barriers with China and was a strong critic of prior administration policy, has been encouraged by what he’s seen.

“It’s a sign he’s, consciously or not, being pragmatic in a constructive way,” Posen said. “American presidents talk tough and threaten China, and in each case they ended up — I think rightly — backing off.”
entries.author: Jeff Stein

entries.title: OpenAI Says Rogue AI Agents Accessed Government Websites
entries.summary: The AI giant's models accessed publicly available information on SEC and U.S. Census Bureau websites.
entries.content:
By Kaitlyn Huamani and Garance Burke

SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — OpenAI disclosed Friday that its artificial intelligence agents had interacted with several U.S. government websites in unexpected ways, discovered as part of an ongoing review into the company's models' unanticipated behavior.

The AI giant's models accessed publicly available information on two websites operated by the Securities and Exchange Commission as well as U.S. Census Bureau data, the company revealed Friday. OpenAI did not find any use of SEC credentials, access to accounts or nonpublic information, changes to SEC data or systems, or evidence of a compromise or vulnerability, the company said.

The disclosure comes at a time of heightened global concerns about AI systems escaping human control and hacking into external websites, as well as industry calls for a slowdown on AI development, which OpenAI has said it supports.

OpenAI spokesperson Liz Bourgeois said in a statement that the lab is continuing to conduct a review of “misaligned model activity" — meaning when AI systems behave in undesired ways — and is notifying organizations when it identifies potential impacts to their systems.

OpenAI's CEO Sam Altman said on social media Friday that there is an “extensive and ongoing review related to our agents’ use of internet access during training and evaluation.”

AI evaluator and research lab Transluce said Friday that through an independent investigation it also found that agents appearing to originate from OpenAI attempted a rudimentary hack on a Department of Education website for the department’s civil rights office, which did not succeed.

The Department of Education's “system operations reviews" found "no evidence of any impact to our website or databases,” a department spokesperson said Friday.

A Transluce spokesperson said as part of its investigation, it came across data on the open web that revealed fresh details about some previously identified OpenAI agents' activities on U.S. government websites and brought it to OpenAI's attention.

Transluce found “additional rogue activity, some of which is not clearly attributable to OpenAI," targeting other government agencies, including the Justice Department and the Commerce Department, as well as some state government websites in California, Maryland, Illinois, Texas and New York. The models were “using sites in unintended ways and sometimes violating explicit usage policies,” Transluce said in a statement.

OpenAI said it is reviewing Transluce’s report.

If OpenAI notifies organizations it identifies as being impacted by unexpected model behavior, that does not mean there was a security incident, the company said, and could identify a design issue or security weakness that impacted organizations want to address.

Most of the activity OpenAI said it has reviewed so far has involved routine research tasks where agents accessed public web content to answer questions, including government websites seen as authoritative sources of public information.

Several companies have disclosed incidents in recent months when they say their models have behaved unpredictably or hacked into other organizations' websites or systems. OpenAI disclosed in July that two of its most capable AI models were responsible for the cyberattack targeting AI startup Hugging Face.

Altman said in his social media post Friday that the Hugging Face incident “is still the most severe event we’ve seen.”

That incident stirred widespread panic in the industry and beyond about AI models going rogue, and several competing AI labs made similar disclosures in the days and weeks that followed. OpenAI most recently shared six reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in AI models and introduced a framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances of what it called misalignment.

entries.title: Trump Calls the Strait of Hormuz 'Trump Strait' After Iran Proposes a Deal
entries.summary: The Truth Social post was the first public indication of the president's thinking after Iran proposed the new deal.
entries.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump has posted an image of the Strait of Hormuz labeled “Trump Strait” shortly after Iran proposed a deal to open the waterway within a week if the U.S. meets certain conditions.

Meanwhile, Iranian media outlets say the country's president has left New York after the United Nations gathering of world leaders that included Iran's indirect talks with the United States. And Saudi Arabia says it has intercepted another missile it blames on Iran -backed Houthis in neighboring Yemen.

Trump posted an image Friday night on his Truth Social platform of the Strait of Hormuz labeled “Trump Strait,” in the first public indication of his thinking after Iran proposed the new deal and suggested it might help Trump ahead of the midterm elections.

The White House on Friday said only that U.S. officials were having positive and constructive conversations with mediators on the Iran war. Earlier in the week, Iran held hours of indirect talks with the U.S.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told journalists Friday night that under Tehran's proposal, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program in seven days if the United States lifts its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waives sanctions on Iranian oil sales and observes a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.

Semiofficial media outlets in Iran reported that President Masoud Pezeshkian has departed New York for Tehran after the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders.

Pezeshkian's speech to the gathering pushed back against Trump's latest threat to “annihilate” the Islamic Republic, but he ended by saying Tehran remains open to diplomacy.

entries.title: After Locking Up Cade Cavalli, the Nats Have More Pitching Fixes in Mind
entries.summary: Paul Toboni says the team, which defeated the Mets 7-6 Friday night, will upgrade the pitching staff and bullpen this offseason.
entries.content:
Late Friday afternoon, a sharply-dressed Cade Cavalli strode into a news conference room inside Nats Park bearing a wide grin. He hunched down at a table next to Paul Toboni, the team’s president of baseball operations, and stared out at a sea of familiar faces staring back at him. His wife and members of his agency sat in the front row to his right, while members of the Nationals’ ownership sat to his left. His teammates quickly filed into the room and scattered along the back wall.

Behind Cavalli, plastered in large white letters, read a three-word phrase: Here to stay. Last week, the organization signed Cavalli to a four-year, $47 million extension, locking in the 28-year-old pitcher with the franchise until 2030 with a player option in 2031.

“It means the world to me that you guys put your trust in me and we can go compete together on the diamond for the next hopefully five years and go do something special,” Cavalli remarked to the Nationals’ ownership group sitting feet away. “Ever since I got drafted here in 2020 it’s been a dream of mine to be able to go not only compete but win games for the Nationals, and I just want to thank you for the opportunity to do that.”

Cavalli’s signing is a breath of fresh air for Nats fans, who have waited since March of 2023 for the organization to sign a player to a contract extension. Washington ranks 24th in the MLB in spending with a $97 million projected payroll in 2026.

The signing is also a signal that the team’s ownership may be ready to invest in a contender after the team fielded one of the most potent offenses in baseball but missed the playoffs for the seventh-straight season.

“It wasn’t just like a ‘Oh sure, you can do this,’” said Toboni, reflecting on his conversations with ownership during Cavalli’s extension process. “It was like, ‘Heck yeah, this is the type of stuff that we want to be doing.’”

Minutes later, Nationals manager Blake Butera entered the same press conference room with a matching smile on his face.

“As you can tell, I’m in a really good mood today,” Butera joked.

With Cavalli signed, the Nats can turn their attention to what is poised to be an offseason of change. One of the Nats’ chief concerns, Butera put bluntly, is the team’s bullpen rotation, a unit that has given the team headaches at a historic rate late in games.

The Nats are up to 42 blown saves this season with two games still left to play, shattering the previous MLB record of 37 blown saves by the 2024 Chicago White Sox.

“I think if we had an average bullpen, I think we’re probably talking about who we’re playing this weekend,” Butera said. “Whether it’s personnel, whether it’s roles, whatever it might be, we’re going to spend a lot of time on the bullpen this offseason.”

Toboni expressed confidence in the futures of Cavalli and Andrew Alvarez, who started in the Nationals’ win over the Mets Friday night (which also featured the first career save for Josiah Gray). He also expressed an optimism in 24-year-old Connelly Early, whom the Nats acquired via trade in July for infielder Curtis Mead.

“Beyond that, we’re going to be pretty open-minded,” Toboni said. “What is involved there too is not just like ‘Are we going to go outside and sign players?’ but [also] we have a number of pitchers on our staff that are at inflection points in their career… We want the process of really developing this offseason to be really dialed, and I think our guys are bought into that.’”

What Butera and Toboni can hang their hats on following a 75-plus win season is that the organization rosters an offensive nucleus loaded with talent. Between James Wood and C.J. Abrams becoming national names to the development of Cavalli and Daylen Lile into reliable standouts, next year’s iteration of the Nationals brings intrigue and loftier goals.

For Cavalli, that means playoff baseball.

Hours after celebrating his extension, a contract earned after he battled back from Tommy John surgery to become one of the most reliable pitchers in baseball, Cavalli swapped out his suit for a long-sleeved shirt and baseball cap. He stood in the dugout and felt the early-fall breeze swirl over Nats Park, the ballpark he’s expected to excite for the next half-decade of his major league career.

“We’re walking around here feeling the weather, it feels like playoff baseball weather,” Cavalli said. “We’re planning on playing in it next year, and I know that every guy feels it and thinks that.”
